claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning framework will combine local atomic-disorder descriptors with explicit defect- and oxygen-scattering corrections.
The hybrid framework will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity more accurately than analytical models that assume perfect crystals.
The proposed accuracy advantage will apply particularly in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr has inherent configurational disorder.
The samples include a nearly stoichiometric HfNbTaTiZr variant and a variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will be trained using atomistic simulations and experimental data.
The model will explicitly incorporate local chemical-environment descriptors and defect-scattering parameters.
Quantum defect scattering is significant in HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K.
Thermal transport at 300–1200 K is dominated by phonon and impurity scattering.
Local atomic configurations and the spatial distribution of defects, including oxygen-induced point defects, modulate phonon transport and thermal conductivity.
Representing intrinsic disorder and extrinsic-impurity scattering will capture effects overlooked by defect-free analytical models.
Capturing these scattering effects will reduce systematic thermal-conductivity prediction errors.
The hybrid model will predict thermal conductivity within approximately 10% of experiment across both specified temperature regimes.
Traditional analytical predictions can deviate from experiment by more than 25%.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Applicability outside the specified temperature ranges or above 1 wt.% oxygen is uncertain.
Unmodeled defect interactions and scattering mechanisms may change the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
